microcosm: Minicosm is Olesch's own remake of the game Microcosm.
The original's hidden cheats still work: hold S+U+P to make every Duk super, T+A+X for 10000 money, or A+R+M for the hardest meteors.
The second ship is advertised for 5000 and you need that much to buy it, but only 3000 is actually charged.
atoms: A bomb removes only the atom itself: its neighbours keep their bonds pointing at the empty cell, waiting for a matching atom.
The 'fewer 4s' option uses a little dice trick, rand(3,13)/3, which makes four-bond atoms appear about 18% of the time instead of 25%.
Olesch wrote hiscore saving for both modes but commented it out; this version switches it back on as 'Rekord'.
castle: The signature brick in the bottom-right corner of every room has a typo in Olesch's name, and he has no idea how it happened.
Holding Alt+Ctrl is a hidden cheat that lets the hero walk straight through closed trapdoors.
The Ork hero shoots arrows that have no graphic, so his shots fly at you invisibly.
Picking up the arrows a dead archer dropped clears the wrong map cell, so it can make an object next to them vanish. Olesch's own code comment from back then just says "Arrows appear twice".
siege: Siege is a clone of Siege by Fallen Angel Games.
The recipe code is headed 'DAS ZAUBERBUCH!' (the spell book), and the comments for the elephant and the golem both warn: 'He is big, watch out!'
A complete computer opponent is written in the code, but its single start line is commented out, so Siege is strictly two players.
s-type: The original cheats work: hold O (once O+L+E+G, until Olesch shortened it) to max out every weapon and pile up lives, or hold A+L+E+X to summon extra enemy snakes.
Slot 10 of the buy line does nothing at all; you have to pass it to reach the companion pods at slot 11.
huhnshot: Shooting the clock in the top-left corner ('Uhr abgeknallt!', clock shot down) gives 10 extra seconds and 100 points.
Destroying all the hills sets off an avalanche ('LAWINE!!') that drives eight more birds into the sky.
Find every bonus and you unlock a secret machine-gun mode: hold M+G and keep the mouse button down.
lommings: A comment proudly calls O 'THE SUPER-BOOSTER-SPEED-KEY!!!' (five steps per frame), and holding G together with it is a cheat that wins the level instantly.
The + key makes lemmings come out slower and - makes them faster, the reverse of what you'd expect.
The nuke also hits lemmings that are already safe in the exit, turning them into dead ones, so your saved count can drop.
stranded: You can craft an axe, a fishing rod and a hammer, but chopping, fishing and building were never written, so the tools do nothing.
There is no game over: at zero health the hero just looks dead and you can keep on playing.
The radar's hero marker had no graphic in the original, so you could never see yourself on the map; this version adds a red dot.
heatfighter: Heatfighter was an attempt to remake the fighting game MindArms.
The title in the source reads 'Heatfighter: Coolfighter in 2d'.
The 'Template' fighter has no pictures for its special and low attacks, so it turns invisible while doing them, just like in the original.
miniship: Quitting the original said goodbye with 'May the force be with you!', and the fastest energy-recharge setting is simply called 'Starwars'.
The planet's pull uses Newton's law of gravity; Olesch wrote the formula as a comment at the top of the code.
A mix-up in the computer players' aiming makes them thrust almost constantly, so their energy bars spend much of the game near zero.
gigamaze: GigaMaze is a remake of the DOS game MegaMaze, which ran far too fast on newer PCs: Olesch and his brothers played it with a slowdown program, and Olesch wanted a better version, but it was never finished.
The top exit wraps to the bottom, but the bottom gap is much narrower, so a ship that leaves the wrong way ends up stuck in the wall for good.
The code has pickups for a red laser, a stunner, a nuke and 'Life+50' (which actually hands out weapon 5), but none of them ever fire anything.
canonball-riding: Canonball Riding and Ship Duel were the first two games Olesch considered good and finished.
Your score is simply the number of cannonballs fired while you survive.
The cannons speed up from one shot every 2 seconds to one every few frames, and quitting once said 'Ride Canonballs again soon!'
wormbattlewarriors: The original was never finished: player 2's worms start with 500 action points as a test, yet player 2 never gets a turn.
Where combat should be, the code only has the comment 'Interaktion muss kommen!' (interaction has to come); the fighting in this version is new.
Worms that drop down a hole can never climb back up, because the way up is just an empty comment.
baller: Each level carries its own physics settings, such as gravity, friction and the pull of the holes, hidden in the colours of the first few pixels of the level picture.
The losing message really says 'You LOOSE', a typo kept from the original.
A to-do list at the top of the code planned cannons, new terrains and a two-player mode that never arrived.
bunnyjumpers: A commented-out loop in the code would have filled the screen with 10 extra bunnies at random spots.
A 'TODESCRASH' (death crash) block was meant to let one bunny stomp the other, but it never worked, so bunnies can only bounce off each other sideways.
Platforms only catch falling bunnies: a bunny on its way up jumps straight through them.
pingpong: Instead of one ball there are 70, released in pairs, all bouncing at once.
The player who is behind gets 3 points per goal and the leader only 2, and the score is never shown: you just see the banner when someone is 500 ahead.
The code contains a computer player for the bats, but both bats are always set to human.
ship-duel: Ship Duel and Canonball Riding were the first two games Olesch considered good and finished.
The settings screen has 14 values, from lives to the 'Spielerexplosionsdurchmesser' (player explosion diameter), and nothing stops you setting them to zero or below.
The explosion shot was meant to cost mana, but mana was never used: you only need to hold fire for about 2.5 seconds, and it destroys shots but never ships.
thursday-panzers: The teams are uneven: the green computer tanks line up every 80 pixels, the red ones every 60, so red gets 27 tanks against green's 21.
At start the whole 1600x1200 battlefield is painted pixel by pixel with random shades of green, almost two million pixels.
A commented-out mode would have dropped a fresh tank for each team at a random spot every second.
sniper: The header still credits Antonio Marchal's 1997 DIV tutorial, and the old tutorial's asteroid code is still in the file, unused.
All 17 snipers fire together and each one kicks the aim with recoil, so after every salvo the crosshair snaps to the top-left corner.
A minigun sniper and a grenade-launcher sniper with smoke exist in the code, but they are never put on the field.
hatsch1: The longer you hold fire, the bigger and stronger the shot, and the harder its recoil throws your ship backwards.
In the original, ship 3 started exactly on top of ship 2; it now starts in the bottom-left corner.
Commented-out code would have made ships randomly clone themselves and big shots split in two.
runner: Runner was written by Olesch together with Lukas Schw.
Pressing your keys before 'LOS' is a false start that freezes your runner for the entire race.
One second on the race clock is 25 frames instead of 24, so the timer runs about 4% slow.
decathlon: Despite the name, only one of the ten events was ever made: the hammer throw.
The record that ships with the game, 1004, comes straight from Olesch's original save file.
If you never let go, the arm swings all the way round and the hammer is released by force.
ballkill: Your only defence besides the pin is a hair dryer at the top of the screen that can blow rising balls back down.
Olesch's line to load the hiscore was commented out, so the original always started from 0; this version keeps your best score.
After Game Over the original quit to DOS with the message 'Nice playing'.
tron: The game was built on top of DIV's asteroids tutorial: its header still names the tutorial, and the old asteroid code is left in, commented out.
One stray pixel hidden in the background at (673,190) kills any cycle that runs into it.
Commented-out code would have made a cycle speed up when riding close to a trail, a kind of slipstream.
fort: The zig-zag enemies always start by flying to the right, wherever they appear, before turning towards the fort.
Normal enemies shrink as they get closer to the fort.
The original counted the damage to the fort in a hidden variable, so nothing on screen reacted to hits; the 'Schaden' counter is new.
rubik: Despite the name, this is a flat 3x3 grid of numbers whose rows and columns rotate like the slices of a Rubik's cube.
Every game starts just one random move away from solved.
Solving the puzzle sets off a swarm of drifting, colour-changing dots that stays only as long as the numbers are in order.
panzers: The original also painted the tanks with the same random greens as the lawn, making them almost invisible; this version shows them normally.
There is no damage: shells fly straight through tanks, and holding fire shoots one shell every frame, 24 per second.
Tanks can drive off the screen and never come back.
snake: Snake started as DIV's 'Tutorial 4' by Daniel Navarro Medrano, which Olesch modified.
The tutorial allowed up to three apples at once; Olesch changed it to a single apple.
The original put the play field outside its frame graphic, so the worm started next to the frame; this version moves it inside.
kochkurve: Key 2 says 'Koch' but draws the Sierpinski triangle again: the key-1 code was copied and the Koch curve routine was never finished.
The program loads a full-screen 'Mandelbrot' picture that is completely transparent, plus an overlay it never shows, both leftovers from the Mandelbrot program.
About 1,100 recursive steps start roughly 3,300 line-drawing processes, and all of them finish within one single frame.
rotators: The program is still called 'Tutorial 1' and keeps the spaceship tutorial's comments, like 'Prints ship's graphic on screen', plus an unused screen-wrap routine.
A hidden 'Table' speed mode reads past the end of its 13-entry speed list, so the outer keys pick up speeds from unrelated settings and barely move.
Each new key starts moving before the one it hangs on has a position, so every pattern begins with a few stray dots in the top-left corner.
mandelbrot: In preview mode the original calculates every point nine times, once for each pixel of its 3x3 block, and gets the same answer every time.
Keys 3 and 4 change a 'painting' setting that does nothing, because the colour formula that used it was commented out.
Every single point of the picture was its own little DIV process, and the maths runs on whole numbers only, so very deep zooms overflow into strange glitches.
castedit: Before Castle, Olesch hard-coded every level straight into the game code; Castle was the first game he built a level editor for, itself written in DIV as well.
Every Castle room has a brick in the bottom-right corner with Olesch's signature on it, and the editor always draws it there.
Picking an empty slot in the item chooser painted an invisible junk number into the level, and the real Castle level files still contain 11 of these hidden values.
antjumper: The ant's picture in the original is a 1024x768 image that is completely black.
A one-entry slip in the colour table (colour 1 instead of 15) means the ant never sees the white it paints, so it draws a straight line and walks off the screen.
Four extra ants were commented out, each with a direction 0-3, but that number would have set their scheduling priority instead, so all of them would have walked straight up.
balls: Only the right-edge option of the spawn code releases four balls instead of one, so the tree always grows lopsided toward the right.
Each step is rounded down to whole tenths of a pixel, so balls can only fly in a few dozen directions and many early balls miss the centre and fly off the screen.
A 'Kill' flag is set on the line right after the loop ends, so it never runs: after a few minutes the original was quietly keeping thousands of frozen balls alive.
siedler: The minimap in the corner is the game's actual memory: the program stores every settler's job in that image, one pixel per settler.
A misplaced bracket, Rand(0,250==0), means the planned 1-in-251 chance for workers to give up their job can never happen.
About 200 trees along the river are invisible: a line meant to forget trees on water erases the ground under them instead, so settlers can then walk on the river.
